subsystems.name: Chaser spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: carries the capture payload and provides power, propulsion and control.

subsystems.name: Rendezvous and navigation
subsystems.role: finds, tracks and safely approaches a non-cooperative object.

subsystems.name: Capture mechanism
subsystems.role: secures the target so it can be controlled.

subsystems.name: De-orbit system
subsystems.role: lowers the combined stack's orbit so it burns up in the atmosphere.

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: tracks objects, commands the mission and coordinates space traffic.

buildSteps.title: Choose the target
buildSteps.detail: Use space-surveillance catalogues to select a large derelict, such as a defunct satellite or spent upper stage, in a crowded low orbit where removal matters most.

buildSteps.title: Design the capture method
buildSteps.detail: The object is likely tumbling and its shape may be unknown, so net or harpoon suits large bulky targets while a robotic arm suits ones with known features; a magnetic plate works only if the target has a compatible interface.

buildSteps.title: Build the chaser spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: Assemble a bus with solar arrays, batteries, star trackers and enough propulsion to match the target's orbit and later de-orbit the combined mass.

buildSteps.title: Integrate sensors and autonomy
buildSteps.detail: Fit cameras and LiDAR plus software that can close the last few hundred metres without a human in the loop, because radio delays make manual control too slow.

buildSteps.title: Test the capture payload
buildSteps.detail: Exercise the net, harpoon or arm on air-bearing tables that mimic weightlessness, then in thermal-vacuum chambers that mimic space.

buildSteps.title: Launch and commission
buildSteps.detail: Ride-share to an orbit near the target, then check out power, propulsion and sensors over several weeks.

buildSteps.title: Rendezvous and inspect
buildSteps.detail: Drift up to the target, fly around it to map its shape and measure its spin, keeping a safe stand-off distance.

buildSteps.title: Capture and stabilise
buildSteps.detail: Match the target's rotation, deploy the capture device, then damp the combined stack so it can be steered.

buildSteps.title: De-orbit and dispose
buildSteps.detail: Fire thrusters to lower the perigee into the atmosphere, where the target burns up; the chaser either releases first or re-enters with it.

prerequisites.why: you cannot remove what you cannot find and track, and many small objects are still untracked.
demonstrated with cooperative targets and some inspection of non-cooperative ones, but close capture without human control remains risky.
nets and harpoons have been demonstrated in orbit, but not yet used to de-orbit a real derelict.
thrusters, drag sails and tethers can lower an orbit, though the added mass of a captured object demands extra performance.

prerequisites.tech: Standard grapple fixtures on new satellites
prerequisites.why: future spacecraft need a common interface so they can be captured and removed more easily.

pathway.milestone: demonstration missions such as RemoveDEBRIS (2018), ELSA-d (2021) and ADRAS-J (2024)
pathway.unlocks: confidence in net, harpoon, magnetic capture and close inspection.

pathway.milestone: a commercial mission to remove one large derelict
pathway.unlocks: proof that removal can be done end-to-end.

pathway.milestone: multi-target removal and standard grapple fixtures on new satellites
pathway.unlocks: lower cost per object removed and easier future servicing.

pathway.milestone: routine removal tied to launch licensing
pathway.unlocks: stabilising the most crowded orbits and reducing Kessler-syndrome risk.
